Larimer County by the numbers

Where is Larimer County, Colorado, and what shapes its housing?

Larimer County sits at the northern end of the Front Range, along the Wyoming border, and covers 2,634 square miles. Fort Collins is the county seat and its largest city. The 2020 census counted 359,066 residents.

Other communities include Loveland, Estes Park, Berthoud, Johnstown, Timnath, Wellington and Windsor, with Berthoud, Johnstown and Windsor reaching into Weld County. The county was created on November 1, 1861 and named for William Larimer, Jr., the founder of Denver.

Settlement here followed irrigation more than mining. Camp Collins grew into Fort Collins after an 1864 flood, the railroad came in 1877, sugar beets arrived in 1902 with a Great Western Sugar plant in Loveland, and the Colorado Big Thompson Project of the 1930s widened irrigated farmland. For owners, that history explains the mix of city lots, farm parcels and mountain cabins on one tax roll.

What does the Larimer County economy look like?

Colorado State University is the largest employer in Fort Collins, and the city also draws health care, public schools, government and manufacturing jobs. A 2024 city report listed these top Fort Collins employers.

EmployerEmployees
Colorado State University8,850

Interstate 25 runs along the east side of Fort Collins, US 287 becomes College Avenue, and the MAX bus line serves the Mason Corridor. Denver International Airport is about 70 miles south.

Which Larimer County offices handle property tax?

The Assessor values property and takes protests. The Treasurer, who also serves as Public Trustee, mails statements and collects payment. Both offices are at 200 W. Oak Street in Fort Collins.

  • Treasurer and Public Trustee: Suite 2100, (970) 498-7020, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., Monday through Friday. Mailing address is P.O. Box 1250, Fort Collins, CO 80522.
  • Assessor: second floor, (970) 498-7050, same weekday hours. Mailing address is P.O. Box 1190.
  • Title companies can use the Treasury's CTD login, and mortgage servicers have a mass payment option.

The Treasurer states that it does not determine the amount of tax. Questions about value go to the Assessor, and the rate comes from the cities, county, schools and districts that tax your address.

How is a Larimer County tax bill calculated?

The bill is assessed value times the mill levy, and assessed value is actual value times an assessment rate. For 2026 the county's guide lists residential rates of 6.8% for local government and 7.05% for schools, the first year residential property has two rates.

Step in the county's $275,000 exampleResult
Local government: $275,000 x 0.068, then x 0.023425$438.05
Schools: $275,000 x 0.0705, then x 0.052116$1,010.43
Total in the example$1,448.48

That example is a teaching figure from the county, not a quote for your house. Your own levy depends on every district on your bill. The county's guide to Colorado property taxes walks through the same math.

How does Larimer County value homes?

Real property is revalued in odd numbered years. Residential values for 2025 and 2026 rest on market conditions at June 30, 2024, using a 24 month sales study from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024. Vacant and commercial land uses 60 months of sales.

Two details matter to sellers. Foreclosure transfers to lenders are left out of the study, though resales of foreclosed homes are generally used. And the Assessor measures square footage from exterior dimensions, so a builder's interior figure may not match the county record.

Because 2026 is an intervening year, Notices of Valuation usually mail only when value or classification changed.

How do I protest a Larimer County valuation?

Protests are accepted from May 1 through June 8. You can file by mail, an online tool the county says takes 15 minutes or less, in person, by phone or appointment, by fax at 970-498-7070, or at the secure drop box at the southwest entrance of 200 W. Oak Street.

The county's 2026 assessor calendar sets the next steps: Notices of Determination by June 30, County Board of Equalization hearings from July 1 to August 5, and a July 15 deadline to appeal to that board. An alternate protest period runs later, with hearings from September 1 to November 2 and an appeal deadline of September 15.

You can only contest value or classification. Levies are set by the taxing districts, not by the Assessor.

What are the Larimer County payment options?

Taxes for 2025 were due in two equal installments, by the end of February and June 15, or in one payment by April 30. Partial payments are not accepted, and the county notes that amounts of $25 or less are due in full by April 30.

  • Pay online through the Treasury's payment system and print a receipt.
  • Sign up for eNotices and email reminders.
  • Use EquaPay for automated monthly payments if no mortgage escrow covers the taxes.
  • Ask about relief programs: senior exemption, veteran with a disability exemption, deferral, work off program, and the property tax, rent and heat rebate.

What happens at the Larimer County tax lien sale?

Unpaid real property taxes go to a public lien sale. The 2026 sale is scheduled for Thursday, November 19, 2026 at the Larimer County Fairgrounds at the Ranch, 5280 Arena Circle, Loveland, with registration at 7:30 a.m. It is held in person, not online.

The 2026 investor rate is 13%, which state law sets as the federal discount rate on September 1 plus nine points. The advertising list is posted online in early October and updated nightly. Tax sale certificates cancel automatically after fifteen years.

The sale page did not state a redemption period, so ask the Treasurer for the timing on any lien against your house.

How do wildfire and flood history affect Larimer County sellers?

The Cameron Peak fire started August 13, 2020 in Roosevelt National Forest and was declared fully contained on December 2, 2020. It burned 208,663 acres and destroyed 469 structures, including 42 primary residences, and at one point reached within four miles of Loveland.

A Forest Service report cited in that account found that 36% of the burned land had high soil burn severity, with a high risk of erosion or flooding. Owners in Poudre Canyon, Red Feather Lakes, Redstone Canyon and Storm Mountain should expect buyers and insurers to ask about burn scar and defensible space.

Fort Collins itself has a cold semi-arid climate, with about 51 inches of snow and 16 inches of precipitation in an average year.

What do Larimer County sellers face with back taxes or an inherited house?

The common problems are a delinquent bill, a title that needs a probate step, and a roof or foundation that makes a retail listing hard. A cash buyer can buy the house as it stands, but any tax lien still gets paid out of proceeds at closing, so get a payoff figure from the Treasurer at (970) 498-7020 first.

More questions about Larimer County, CO Property Tax Guide

When are Larimer County property taxes due?

For 2025 taxes payable in 2026, the first half was due February 28, the second half June 15 and a single full payment April 30. If a date falls on a non business day, it moves to the next business day.

What is the Larimer County property tax protest deadline?

Protests to the Assessor are accepted May 1 through June 8. You can file by mail, online, in person, by phone or fax, or at the drop box at 200 W. Oak Street.

Does Larimer County run its tax lien sale online?

No. The 2026 sale is in person at the Larimer County Fairgrounds at the Ranch in Loveland on November 19, 2026.

How are Larimer County homes valued for 2026?

2026 is an intervening year, so residential values still reflect the June 30, 2024 appraisal date and a sales study from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024.

Who sets my Larimer County tax rate?

Taxing authorities such as cities, the county, school districts and fire districts set levies. The Assessor sets value and the Treasurer collects the bill.

Denver County by the numbers

What is Denver County, and how does it differ from other Colorado counties?

Denver County is a consolidated city and county, so one government handles what a city and a county do elsewhere. It was formed when the City of Denver merged with Arapahoe County on December 1, 1902.

The settlement dates to November 1858, during the Gold Rush, and Denver City was incorporated on November 7, 1861. The county covers 154.7 square miles at an average elevation of 5,280 feet, which is where the Mile High City name comes from.

For a homeowner, the practical result is simple. There is no separate city tax bill and county tax bill. The City and County of Denver runs both the valuation office and the collection office, and both sit inside the Department of Finance.

How is Denver laid out, and what are the neighborhoods?

Denver is organized into 78 official neighborhoods, which grew out of the 1970 statistical neighborhoods, and 19 larger planning areas.

Residents also use informal names that do not match the official map exactly. Well-known ones include:

  • LoDo, Uptown and the Golden Triangle near downtown
  • RiNo, Curtis Park and Park Hill
  • Central Park, the former Stapleton area, renamed in 2020

The old Stapleton International Airport site was redeveloped into the Central Park neighborhood. Denver International Airport is the city's weather station and lies about 20 miles from downtown.

Why this matters when you sell: a house in one neighborhood can sit in a different school boundary, tax area or special district than one a few blocks away. Your tax bill lists the taxing authorities that apply to your parcel.

Who values the house and who collects the tax in Denver?

The Denver Assessor sets the value of your property, and the Treasury division collects the money. Neither office sets the tax rate.

Office or itemRole or figure
Assessor's OfficeValues real property, mails Notices of Valuation, takes protests
TreasuryMails statements and collects payments, runs the delinquent list and tax lien sale
Taxing authoritiesSet mill levies each December
Denver's 2024 combined general levy79.202 mills (0.079202)

The City and County of Denver states plainly that the Assessor does not set tax rates or collect payments. If your bill looks too high, the first question is whether the value is wrong (an Assessor matter) or the levy is higher (a taxing-authority matter).

How does Denver value a house and calculate the bill?

Denver values homes by comparing them with recent sales of similar homes, and it reappraises every two years in odd-numbered years such as 2023 and 2025.

The 2025 values use sales from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024. Commercial and industrial property uses cost, market and income approaches, and business personal property is valued from what owners declare.

The formula on Denver's assessment page is: (actual value minus value reduction) times assessment rate times mill levy.

2024 property typeValue reduction per parcelAssessment rate
Residential$55,0006.7%
Commercial improved$30,00027.9%
All other$027.9%

Those are Denver's 2024 figures. The state Division of Property Taxation lists different rates for 2026: 6.8% for residential local government levies and 7.05% for residential school levies. Colorado now uses two residential rates, one for local governments and one for schools. Check your Notice of Valuation and bill for the year you are in.

How do I protest a Denver property valuation?

File your protest by June 8 each year. If that date falls on a weekend or holiday, it moves to the next business day.

The Assessor mails a Notice of Valuation with instructions, and you can protest in writing, in person or over the internet. A strong protest includes:

  • Your parcel or schedule number from the notice and a daytime phone number
  • Your reasons, stated plainly
  • Evidence such as comparable sales or documented condition problems

If you missed a past year, Denver says you can go back up to two prior years by filing a Board of County Commissioners petition for abatement or refund of taxes.

If you disagree with the Board's decision, you can appeal to the State Board of Assessment Appeals, to District Court, or to binding arbitration. The state's table also shows that counties with more than 300,000 residents follow the alternate schedule, with Notices of Determination mailed by August 15.

For a seller, a protest filed before listing can matter. A lower value can change the next bill the buyer inherits, and a house with documented repair needs often has a stronger case than a move-in ready one.

What does the Denver property tax calendar look like?

Denver mails statements in January, collects half payments on the last day of February and June 15, and takes full payment by April 30.

WhenWhat happens
JanuaryAnnual statements mailed
Last day of FebruaryFirst half due
April 30Full payment due
By May 1Assessor mails Notices of Valuation
MayDelinquency notices mailed for unpaid taxes
June 15Second half due
September and OctoberDelinquent taxes advertised in a local newspaper

Denver's calendar lists the public auction of real estate tax liens in October. Another county listing says November, so confirm the current date with the Treasury before relying on either.

The calendar also shows that the Assessor mails senior citizen and disabled veteran exemption notices in January, and that applications for the elderly and disabled refund program are due April 30. Deferral applications for seniors and active duty military are due April 1.

Why do weather and hail matter for a Denver house sale?

Denver gets hail often enough that roof condition is usually the first item a buyer or inspector raises.

Denver ranks 10th among U.S. cities of 50,000 or more for hail risk, and three of the ten costliest hailstorms in U.S. history hit it, in 1990, 2009 and 2017.

The rest of the climate is dry and sunny. The city logs about 3,100 hours of sunshine a year, about 14.5 inches of precipitation and about 49 inches of snow at the airport. July highs average 89.9 degrees, December highs average 44 degrees, and the record high is 105 degrees, set June 28, 2018.

A roof with old hail damage, cracked siding or dented gutters lowers what traditional buyers will pay. A cash buyer who accepts the house as it stands removes the repair negotiation.

What drives Denver's economy, and what does it mean for sellers?

Government, schools, health care and aviation employ the most people in Denver, and that steady base supports demand for housing across the city.

The 2023 financial report lists these top employers:

  • City and County of Denver, 13,584
  • Denver Public Schools, 12,693
  • State of Colorado, 10,686
  • Denver Health and Hospital Authority, 9,502
  • United Airlines, 7,230

Metro Denver's GDP was $311.9 billion in 2023, and eight Fortune 500 companies have headquarters in the city. The 2020 census counted 715,522 residents.

For sellers, that employment base means a deep pool of buyers, but also a large number of landlords, heirs and owners of older houses who want a quick sale without repairs.

What should I do if I owe Denver property tax and want to sell?

Start by finding out exactly what is owed, since a delinquent balance carries interest and can end up sold as a tax lien.

The Denver Treasury publishes a delinquent real property list and answers questions at propertytaxinfo@denvergov.org. Send your parcel ID, address and payment dates if you think a delinquent notice is wrong.

  • Pull your current balance before you list or accept an offer
  • Ask whether any prior-year taxes are open as well as the current year
  • Check for service liens, which the Treasury also handles
  • Tell any buyer about the balance up front so it can be settled at closing

A cash sale can close on a short timeline, and the tax balance is paid from the proceeds like any other lien. That keeps the account from falling further behind while you decide.

More questions about Denver County, CO Property Tax Guide

What is the property tax protest deadline in Denver County?

June 8 each year. When June 8 falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline moves to the next business day. The Notice of Valuation explains how to file.

How often does Denver reappraise homes?

Every two years, in odd-numbered years. The 2025 values were based on sales from July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2024.

Who sets the tax rate in Denver?

Taxing authorities set mill levies each December. The Assessor does not set rates or collect payments. Denver's 2024 combined general levy was 79.202 mills.

When are Denver property taxes due?

Half payments are due the last day of February and June 15. Full payment is due April 30.

Can I sell a Denver house if the taxes are unpaid?

Yes. The balance is paid from the sale proceeds. Get the current figure from the Treasury first so there are no surprises at closing.

Boulder County by the numbers

What is Boulder County, and how is property tax run here?

Boulder County is a Front Range county of about 740 square miles whose seat is the City of Boulder. Two elected offices run its property tax: the Assessor sets values, and the Treasurer sends bills and takes payments.

The county touches Larimer County to the north, Weld to the east, Broomfield to the southeast, Jefferson and Gilpin to the south, and Grand County to the west. Its 2020 population was 330,758, and the July 2025 Census estimate is 328,560.

Cities and towns inside it include Boulder, Longmont, Lafayette, Louisville, Erie, Lyons, Nederland, Superior, Jamestown and Ward. Every one of them is billed through the same Treasurer, so a house in Lyons and a house in Lafayette share the same due dates.

What do Census numbers say about Boulder County homes?

The typical owner-occupied home in Boulder County is valued at $756,300 in the Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures. That is the base the tax system works from, so even small rate changes move bills by hundreds of dollars.

Measure (2020 to 2024)Boulder County
Median value of owner-occupied homes$756,300
Owner-occupied housing rate62.0%

Roughly 38% of homes are rented, so many owners are landlords whose tax bills come on top of license and inspection costs in cities like Boulder.

What is the yearly property tax calendar in Boulder County?

Colorado's calendar starts on January 1, the assessment date, and runs through the December levies. The county Assessor's calendar page lays out the steps.

  • January 1: assessment date for all taxable property, and the date the general tax lien attaches.
  • By May 1: Notices of Valuation for real property go out.
  • By June 8: taxpayers file real property appeals.
  • August 25: the Assessor sends the Abstract of Assessment to the state and notifies the taxing entities of their values.
  • By December 15: local entities certify their levies.
  • By December 22: county commissioners levy the taxes.

The calendar says these are statutory dates that apply in any year, and it notes that some counties use an alternate protest procedure with later dates. Boulder County's own appeals page lists an August 15 determination date and a September 15 Board of Equalization deadline.

How is a Boulder County tax bill built?

Each taxing body multiplies its own mill levy by the assessed value, and the bill is the total of those amounts. Assessed value is actual value times a state assessment rate.

Property type2025 rate2026 rate
Residential, school districts7.05%7.05%
Residential, local government6.25%6.8%
Commercial, industrial, vacant land, business personal property27%26%
Agricultural, renewable energy27%25%
Oil and gas production87.5%87.5%

For 2026, the local government side first subtracts 10% of the first $700,000 of a home's actual value. School district math skips that step. On the county's $800,000 example, the local side uses a reduced value of $730,000.

We do not state a county-wide mill levy here, because levies differ by school, fire and special district. The Treasurer's account lookup shows the real figure for any address.

When must you pay Boulder County property tax?

The Boulder County Treasurer lists March 2 and June 15 for half payments, or April 30 for the full amount, for 2026. Checks and money orders go to the Boulder County Treasurer, and cash should not be mailed.

The postmark date counts as the payment date for taxes due this year. Interest on a first-half payment starts at 1% in March and reaches 6% by August. A full payment made in May costs 1%, and 4% by August. A second-half payment made June 16 to 30 costs 1%, and 3% in August.

For September through December, the Treasurer asks you to call. The page also warns that payments after August 1 may carry extra fees.

Where are the Treasurer's offices?

The main Treasurer office is at 1325 Pearl St., first floor, in Boulder, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. A Longmont office at 515 Coffman St., Suite 113, opens on Mondays only.

  • Phone: 303-441-3520
  • Email: treasurer@bouldercounty.gov
  • Mail: P.O. Box 471, Boulder, CO 80306
  • The Lafayette office at 1755 S. Public Road is listed as closed until late January 2027.

The county page says online tax payments are disabled for the rest of the year, though account details and receipts remain viewable. It also shows a payment link, so confirm with the office before relying on either.

How do you appeal your assessment in Boulder County?

Real property appeals are accepted from May 1 through June 8, and late filings forfeit the right to appeal. You can file by email, mail, fax, online, drop box or in person at 1325 Pearl St., second floor.

A strong appeal states the value you believe is right, explains why the Assessor's figure is off, and lists comparable sales with address, price and date. For this cycle the sales window runs July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2024. If few sales exist, verified sales from up to five years earlier can be used.

You can also correct record errors, such as square footage, bedroom and bath count, lot size or basement finish. The Assessor's phone is 303-441-3530, and its email is assessor@bouldercounty.gov.

After the Notice of Determination, you have until September 15 to appeal in writing to the county Board of Equalization. The state calendar then allows 30 days from the board's mailing to go to the State Board of Assessment Appeals, district court or binding arbitration. Business personal property appeals are filed June 15 to June 30.

What happens to unpaid property tax in Boulder County?

Unpaid real property tax can be sold as a tax lien at the county's annual auction. The county's page lists the 2026 sale for November 13, with 13% annual interest on liens sold this year.

The Treasurer posts the properties advertised for sale and updates the spreadsheet each Friday. Delinquent payments must be in certified funds. For a seller, an unpaid balance is a closing item, because the title company will pay it from the proceeds.

How have fire and flood history shaped valuation here?

Boulder County has two recent disasters that affect how parcels are assessed and sold. The Marshall Fire of December 30, 2021 destroyed an estimated 1,084 structures and damaged 149, across 6,026 acres of Boulder County, Louisville and Superior.

The September 2013 flood destroyed 262 homes in the county and damaged nearly 300, with Boulder recording 9.08 inches of rain in a single day. Anyone selling a house with that history should keep repair records, since the assessor's property record and the buyer's questions both start there.

What do Boulder County sellers need to know about tax and closing?

Colorado property tax is paid in arrears, so a house sold in the spring may carry a bill for the prior year. The January 1 lien date is why the closing agent checks the Treasurer's records for any balance.

  • Ask the Treasurer for a payoff figure before setting a closing date.
  • Check your valuation notice each May, since an appeal window is only about five weeks.
  • Keep the Notice of Determination if you appealed, as it shows the value of record.

The county also records the deed at $43 per document plus the state documentary fee of one cent per $100 over $500.

More questions about Boulder County, CO Property Tax Guide

What is the deadline to appeal a Boulder County valuation?

June 8 for real property, with filings dated by 11:59 p.m. that day. The county says the deadline is strictly enforced.

When are Boulder County property taxes due?

For 2026 the Treasurer lists March 2 and June 15 for two half payments, or April 30 for the full amount.

Who sets my Boulder County property value?

The Boulder County Assessor sets it, using sales from the base period of July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2024. The Assessor does not set the tax rate.

Can I appeal my Boulder County tax bill itself?

No. The Assessor says taxes are set by budgeting bodies such as county commissioners, city councils, school boards and special districts. You can appeal the value only.

How much interest applies if I pay late in Boulder County?

It depends on the month and the payment type. A full payment made in May carries 1%, while a first-half payment made in May carries 3%. The Treasurer's table runs through August, and later months need a call to 303-441-3520.

Arapahoe County by the numbers

What is Arapahoe County, Colorado, and where does it sit?

Arapahoe County is a long, narrow county stretching across the southern Denver metro area and out onto the eastern plains. Wikipedia lists Littleton as the county seat, chosen over Englewood in a 1904 vote. The county was organized on November 1, 1861 as one of Colorado's 17 original counties.

It covers 805 square miles, about 72 miles east to west and only 4 to 12 miles north to south. It borders Denver, Adams, Washington, Lincoln, Elbert, Douglas and Jefferson counties. The 2020 census counted 655,070 residents, which made it the third most populous county in the state.

The county's cities and towns include Aurora, Centennial, Cherry Hills Village, Englewood, Greenwood Village, Littleton, Sheridan, Columbine Valley, Deer Trail, Foxfield and Glendale. Glendale is an exclave surrounded by Denver. Bennett, Bow Mar and Strasburg lie partly inside the county.

Public school districtsNine: Aurora, Bennett, Byers, Cherry Creek, Deer Trail, Englewood, Littleton, Sheridan, Strasburg

Which cities in Arapahoe County matter most to a home seller?

Aurora is the biggest, but it is split across three counties. Its 2020 population of 386,261 included 336,035 people in Arapahoe County, 47,720 in Adams County and 2,506 in Douglas County. Aurora is the third most populous city in Colorado and covers about 165 square miles.

Centennial is the other large city. Voters approved its incorporation in 2000 and it became a city on February 7, 2001, formed from unincorporated Arapahoe County including the former Castlewood and Southglenn areas. Wikipedia says it was the largest incorporation in U.S. history at the time. Its 2020 population was 108,418.

Most of Centennial is in Cherry Creek Public Schools, with the western part in Littleton Public Schools. Aurora is served by Aurora Public Schools and, in places, by Bennett and Brighton 27J. If your house sits near a district line, the school assignment can change from one block to the next.

What drives the Arapahoe County economy?

Government, medicine, aerospace and finance anchor the county's job base. In Aurora, the Aurora Economic Development Council ranks Buckley Space Force Base first among public employers, followed by the Anschutz Medical Campus. The campus grew out of Fitzsimons Army Hospital, which opened in 1918 and was decommissioned in 1999.

Centennial's 2023 financial report lists Comcast, United Healthcare, Arrow Electronics, United Launch Alliance, CommonSpirit Health and Sierra Nevada Corporation among its top employers. A seller who is relocating for one of these jobs, or leaving after a layoff, often needs a quick close, which is where a direct cash sale can fit.

How do roads and rail affect homes in Arapahoe County?

Aurora straddles Interstate 70, Interstate 225 and the E-470 beltway. Light rail reached the southwest edge of Aurora on November 17, 2006, with the H Line stopping at the Dayton and Nine Mile stations. The R Line to Peoria Station opened on February 24, 2017, where riders can transfer to the A Line to Denver International Airport.

The eastern edge of Aurora adjoins the Colorado Air and Space Port. Wikipedia also notes that much of Aurora is closer to the airport than to downtown Denver. Houses near stations or highways trade convenience for noise, and buyers price that in.

How did Arapahoe County get its name and its shape?

The county takes its name from the Arapaho Nation. Wikipedia says the name was first used in 1855 for a much larger Kansas Territory county, and the present county calls itself Colorado's First County because its origins predate the Pikes Peak Gold Rush. That older, larger Arapahoe County also produced Adams County, which the legislature carved from it in 1901.

Aurora has its own younger story. It was platted in 1891 as Fletcher, incorporated as a town in 1903, and became the City of Aurora on March 9, 1928. Buckley Field was built by the Army Air Corps in 1942 and later became Buckley Space Force Base.

The county also holds several schools and colleges: the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus and the Community College of Aurora in Aurora, and Arapahoe Community College in Littleton.

When is Arapahoe County property tax due?

Under Colorado law, you can pay the full bill by April 30 or split it in two: the first half by the last day of February and the second half by June 15. This comes from C.R.S. 39-10-104.5, and it applies to Arapahoe County like every other county.

  • First half: last day of February.
  • Second half: June 15.
  • Full payment: April 30, with no interest if paid on time.
  • Interest: one percent per month on late amounts, counting a partial month as a whole month.
  • Totals under $25 must be paid in full by April 30.

A mailed payment is treated as received on the postmark date. If it has no postmark but arrives within five days of the due date, the treasurer records the due date. A weekend or holiday deadline moves to the next business day. Because the state sets these rules, we do not repeat the county's own wording here. How does a property valuation appeal work in Arapahoe County?

You start by telling the assessor you think the value is too high, using the form that comes with your notice of valuation or a written letter. State law lets you object if the property was valued too high, valued twice, or is exempt. The assessor must consider whatever information you present.

If the assessor leaves the value alone, the assessor must give written reasons and mail you two copies of the completed form. A bare denial does not meet that requirement. You can then appeal to the county board of equalization.

The Justia copy of the 2022 statute sets the objection date at June 1 for real property. Counties have since posted later dates; Adams County, for example, lists June 8. We could not open an Arapahoe County page to confirm its current date, so check your notice of valuation for the exact deadline before you rely on any of these numbers.

What happens when Arapahoe County taxes go unpaid, and can I still sell?

Unpaid taxes become a lien that the county can sell. Under C.R.S. 39-11-101, the treasurer must mail each owner of unpaid prior-year taxes a notice no later than September 1. The notice names the amount owed and a payment date at least fifteen days after mailing.

You can still sell a house with taxes owing. The delinquent amount, interest and fees are paid from the proceeds, so ask the title company to request an exact payoff from the treasurer. If the owner has died or is behind on several bills, a buyer who pays cash and closes on your timeline can keep the lien sale from becoming the deciding event.

For an Aurora house, check which county the parcel is in first. A lot in the Adams or Douglas portion has a different treasurer than one in Arapahoe County.

What should an Arapahoe County seller check before closing?

Start with the parcel itself: confirm the county, the school district and the tax bill, since an Aurora address can fall in any of three counties. Then look at how far into the tax calendar you are, because interest builds each month and a closing can land on either side of a deadline.

  • Ask the treasurer for a written payoff of any delinquent tax, interest and fees.
  • Find out whether you paid in two halves or in full, so the title company can credit the right amount.
  • Keep every notice of valuation. If you filed an objection, note the date you filed.
  • If a September notice from the treasurer has arrived, treat the payment date in it as the real deadline.
  • Tell your buyer about any open appeal, since a lowered value affects later bills.

We buy houses in Arapahoe County as they stand. If back taxes, an old roof or a tenant are part of your situation, a cash offer can keep the closing from depending on a lender's schedule.

More questions about Arapahoe County, CO Property Tax Guide

What is the county seat of Arapahoe County?

Littleton is the county seat. Voters chose it over Englewood in 1904.

How many people live in Arapahoe County?

The 2020 census counted 655,070 residents, the third largest county population in Colorado.

When is the second half of property tax due in Arapahoe County?

June 15 under C.R.S. 39-10-104.5. The first half is due the last day of February and a full payment is due April 30.

Is all of Aurora in Arapahoe County?

No. Aurora lies in Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties. In 2020, 336,035 of its 386,261 residents were in Arapahoe County.

What interest applies if I pay late?

One percent per month, with a partial month counted as a full month. A first-half payment made in April, for example, carries 2 percent.

Can I sell my Arapahoe County house if I owe property tax?

Yes. The unpaid tax is typically settled from the sale proceeds at closing after the title company gets a payoff figure from the treasurer.

Eagle County by the numbers

Where is Eagle County, Colorado, and how big is it?

Eagle County is a mountain county of 1,692 square miles in western Colorado, with the Town of Eagle as its seat and Edwards as its largest community.

It was created on February 11, 1883 from part of Summit County and named for the Eagle River. The seat was first Red Cliff and moved to Eagle in 1921. The 2020 census counted 55,731 people, and the 2025 estimate is 54,291, or about 33 per square mile.

Interstate 70 crosses the county east to west. The Eagle River rises in the southeast, takes in Gore Creek at Dowds Junction and joins the Colorado River in the west.

What is the terrain, and who owns the land?

The county runs from 6,128 feet on the Colorado River to 14,011 feet at Mount of the Holy Cross, and much of it is public land.

White River National Forest covers a large share, and the Bureau of Land Management manages much of the rest. Public ownership of that much ground is a reason to check what your parcel borders before you list.

Neighboring counties are Grand, Summit, Lake, Pitkin, Garfield and Routt. Colorado Mountain College has a Vail Valley campus in Edwards. Three school systems reach into the county: Eagle County School District RE-50J, Roaring Fork RE-1 and West Grand 1-JT. RE-50J runs eight elementary, three middle and three high schools.

How does Eagle County assess a home?

The Eagle County Assessor values residential property by the market approach, using verified comparable sales, as of a January 1 assessment date.

The county reappraises in odd-numbered years, and the June 30, 2024 appraisal date applies to tax years 2025 and 2026. Sales data were drawn from the 24 months ending June 30, 2024, or five years when data was thin.

How are Eagle County tax bills calculated, and why did they rise?

Assessed value times the combined mill levy gives the bill, and about 90 taxing authorities set levies across roughly 367 taxing districts in the county.

Local news reported that the 2025 bills rose around 10% or more for many owners. Assessor Mark Chapin said residential values rose 8% under the reappraisal, and a temporary $55,000 value reduction passed in 2024 had expired. The county average levy was about 65 mills, and some metro districts reach 125 mills, such as the Buckhorn area of Gypsum.

Your Tax Area code on the Notice of Valuation, in a format such as 236, P236 or SC236, tells you which authorities apply. The county posts a spreadsheet of taxing authorities by area. Final 2026 amounts depend on December levies, so confirm with the Treasurer in January 2027.

When can I appeal an Eagle County valuation?

  • By mail to Eagle County Assessor, P.O. Box 449, Eagle, CO 81631, or by fax at 970-328-8667
  • An agent needs your written authorization, and you should keep proof of mailing

Good evidence includes an appraisal dated within six months before June 30, 2024, sales details on your property or comparables, or corrections to property details. A follow-up inspection may be needed.

The Assessor mails a Notice of Determination on or before June 30. If you disagree, or hear nothing, file a written appeal with the County Board of Equalization by July 15, 2026. The office phone is 970-328-8640, or toll free 800-225-6136.

When is Eagle County property tax due, and what are the late charges?

Pay in two halves, the last day of February and June 15, or pay everything by April 30.

After August, call the Treasurer's Office for the exact figure. A returned check carries a $20 fee.

What happens to unpaid Eagle County taxes?

Real estate taxes still unpaid at the end of October are sold at the November tax lien sale, usually on the first or second Wednesday.

The county's timeline runs like this:

  • May, June, August and September: calls or emails to delinquent owners when contact details are on file
  • July 31: delinquent notice deadline, and payment by August 1 keeps a lien investor from adding current-year taxes to a prior lien
  • October: unpaid real estate and mobile home taxes are published in the newspaper for three weeks
  • November: the tax lien sale

To redeem a sold lien, payment must reach the Treasurer by the last business day of the month, in cash or certified funds, from the owner of record. Seniors and active military can ask about deferral at colorado.propertytaxdeferral.com or (833) 634-2513.

How do I pay taxes and get figures when selling an Eagle County house?

Call the Treasurer at 970-328-8860 for balances, and email taxcerts@eaglecounty.us to request a tax certificate.

Payment can be made by e-check online for a $1.00 fee, by card online, by check payable to Eagle County Treasurer to PO Box 479, Eagle, CO 81631, or by wire. For wire instructions call 970-328-8868 and verify them by phone, because the county warns of cyber fraud. Bank bill pay can arrive late and unpostmarked, so interest may apply even when you paid on time.

If a lender pays from escrow, the Treasurer cannot send duplicates to the mortgage company, since state law sends statements to the owner of record. The county page does not describe closing payoffs, so ask the office directly.

What do sellers in the Eagle valley usually face?

Sellers here often deal with large levies in some metro districts, reappraisal jumps and mortgage escrow shortfalls, and each of those can complicate a conventional sale.

Owners of inherited homes, out-of-area owners and landlords tend to want a clean exit with no showings. A cash purchase that accepts the house as it is, with tax and any lien paid from proceeds, fits that need. Before you accept any offer, get the Treasurer's balance, confirm your Tax Area, and note whether a Board of Equalization appeal is still open, since a successful appeal lowers the next bill for whoever owns the house.

May 1 through June 8, 2026, postmarked or delivered by June 8. File online at appealeaglecounty.com or use the form on your Notice of Valuation.

Eagle County Treasurer, PO Box 479, Eagle, CO 81631, with your tax coupon and account number.

File a written appeal with the County Board of Equalization by July 15, 2026.

El Paso County by the numbers

Who sets and collects property tax in El Paso County?

Two elected offices split the work. The El Paso County Assessor values property, and the El Paso County Treasurer sends the bills, collects the money and passes it on to every taxing district. Neither office sets the rate you pay.

The Colorado General Assembly sets the assessment rate, and each taxing authority sets its own mill levy every year. The Assessor's page says the levy is the share of the bill going to schools, fire districts, water and sanitation districts, library districts, other agencies and special districts. Because every district is different, two houses a few miles apart can get different bills. The Treasurer's office says it distributes county-collected revenue to more than 300 local taxing entities each month.

The Treasurer explains that property taxes are collected in arrears. A bill that arrives in January covers the previous tax year. A payment must be received by the office or carry a postmark dated no later than the due date, until the after September 30 rule starts.

How does the El Paso County tax lien sale work?

The county holds an annual tax lien auction for unpaid real estate taxes. For 2026, the Treasurer reports that every real estate account with a balance through October 23, 2026 had a lien placed through the sale held October 28, 2026.

Owners of those parcels can find the payoff amount by calling (719) 520-7900. The office also describes a treasurer's deed process, which is the later step if a lien is never redeemed. Redemption payments must reach the Treasurer on or before the last business day of the month.

For a seller, the Treasurer's tax certificate is the document that shows the current status of the account, including any outstanding amount.

How are El Paso County homes reappraised?

Colorado reappraises all real property in odd-numbered years, and El Paso County mails a Notice of Valuation shortly after May 1 of those years. For tax year 2026, the Assessor says 2025 values are in effect, built on a base year of 2023.

The Assessor reported 283,492 active real property parcels in 2023, including mobile homes, which is why the office uses mass appraisal. Residential property can only be valued by the market approach under state law. In the Assessor's words, a square foot value is not the market approach.

Staff appraisers follow building permits for garages, decks, finished basements and additions, and they also track demolitions and fires that lower value. The data collection period used for 2025 and 2026 values ran from January 1, 2023 through June 30, 2024, citing Colorado Statute 39-1-104(12.3)(a).

How do I appeal an El Paso County assessment?

The formal appeal window runs May 1 to June 8. An appeal can be filed online through the Assessor's property record search, by phone, by mail, in person or by fax, and the back of the Notice of Valuation is the official appeal form.

  • Find your 10-digit parcel number in the upper left of the notice.
  • File separately for each parcel, with its own documents, even if the evidence is identical.
  • Include a recent appraisal, photos, comparable sales or a written description of the condition.
  • Surrender all documentation when you file.
  • Keep proof of mailing.

The Assessor responds in writing with a Notice of Determination on or before August 15. If you disagree, the next step is the County Board of Equalization at 1675 W. Garden of the Gods Road. After that, an owner may go to the Board of Assessment Appeals, district court or binding arbitration with the county commissioners. Each step after the CBOE decision must be started within 30 days of the decision letter. Binding arbitration results are final.

What tax paperwork is needed to sell a house in El Paso County?

The main document is a Certificate of Taxes Due, which shows whether taxes on a parcel are owed or paid. The Treasurer charges $10 per certificate.

  • Title and settlement companies can use the county's CTD portal, a subscription service with a $500 setup fee, a $500 annual renewal, and $10 per certificate.
  • Anyone else can mail the request form with a $10 check payable to El Paso County Treasurer, Attn: Tax Certificates.
  • The office asks for 48 hours of processing after it receives a mailed request.

The county notes that the website shows only the current billing cycle and may not show prior or future balances, such as special assessments billed later. A signed certificate showing all taxes paid and tax sales redeemed is conclusive evidence that the parcel was free of property taxes at that time. Sellers should ask for the certificate rather than relying on the online search alone.

What payment options does the El Paso County Treasurer offer?

Owners can pay online through the county's payment portal or by mail. The Treasurer also lists EquaPay, a program that lets owners prepay their taxes in monthly installments, and an option for electronic statement delivery.

A Tax History Dashboard was launched to give the public more access to property tax information. Mailing addresses for tax statements come from the Assessor, so an address change goes through the Assessor's change of address form and transfers to the Treasurer automatically. The Treasurer's office says to complete its electronic delivery form to enroll for future tax years.

Prepayment of taxes must be received by noon on the last business day of December, and payments after that bear a January receipt date.

What is El Paso County like beyond the tax bill?

El Paso County covers 2,127 square miles of land, from the Pikes Peak foothills on the west to farm and ranch land in the east. The Assessor says agricultural land is mostly in the eastern part of the county and must meet strict criteria for the agricultural classification, while mountain parcels can be affected by topography and access.

Growth has been steady. The county had 987 people in 1870, 143,742 in 1960, 516,929 in 2000 and 730,395 in 2020, with a 2025 estimate of 757,040. There are 17 public school districts in the county, and Colorado Springs School District 11 and Academy School District 20 are both among its top ten employers. Colleges include the U.S. Air Force Academy, the University of Colorado Colorado Springs, Colorado College and Pikes Peak State College.

More questions about El Paso County, CO Property Tax Guide

When is the El Paso County property tax due?

The first half is due the last day of February, the full payment is due April 30, and the second half is due June 15. A date that falls on a weekend or holiday moves to the next business day.

What is the deadline to appeal an El Paso County valuation?

The appeal period runs from May 1 to June 8, after the Notice of Valuation is mailed shortly after May 1. The Assessor replies with a Notice of Determination by August 15.

How much is a Certificate of Taxes Due in El Paso County?

It costs $10 per certificate. Mail requests need a check for each request, and the office asks for 48 hours of processing.

What happens if I miss the June 15 payment?

Unpaid taxes become delinquent after the second half deadline, delinquent notices go out in July with interest and charges, and unpaid real estate taxes are advertised in September and sold at auction in October.

Can I sell my El Paso County house if taxes are owed?

Yes. Taxes owed are shown on the tax certificate the title company orders, and the balance is settled at closing. If a tax lien has already been sold, call the Treasurer at (719) 520-7900 for the payoff amount.

Who do I call about my property value versus my tax bill?

Call the Assessor at (719) 520-6600 about value, classification and appeals. Call the Treasurer at (719) 520-7900 about payments, statements, liens and certificates.

Median value is a county-wide midpoint. A small house in Delta and an orchard property near Paonia will not land near it, and the tax bill follows the property's own assessed value.

How do you get around Delta County and reach an airport?

US 50 runs through Delta as Main Street and connects it to Montrose and Grand Junction. State Highway 65 climbs north over Grand Mesa toward I-70, and State Highway 92 starts in Delta and runs east for 73 miles.

Montrose Regional Airport is about 21 miles south of Delta, and Grand Junction, 39 miles north, has scheduled flights and an Amtrak station.

How does Delta County calculate property tax?

Delta County multiplies actual value by an assessment rate, then applies the mill levies of every taxing authority in the property's tax area. The county's property tax explainer walks through each step.

  1. The Assessor classifies the property by its use on January 1.
  2. Residential actual value comes from comparable sales only. For tax years 2025 and 2026 those sales fall between July 1, 2022 and June 30, 2024.
  3. Starting in 2025, residential property has two assessment rates, one for the school district and one for other local governments. The county's 2025 example uses 6.25 percent for local governments and 7.05 percent for schools.
  4. Each taxing authority divides its revenue need by the assessed value inside its boundary to set a mill levy.

The county's worked example uses a $275,000 home and lands at $1,164.61 in total tax. It is an illustration with example levies, so use your own bill for a real number. All of the property tax stays in the county and none funds state services.

What are the Delta County property tax dates?

Taxes are billed for the prior year, and you can pay in full by April 30 or in two halves. The dates below come from the Delta County pages.

ItemDate
Notice of Valuation, real propertyBy May 1
Protest of real property valueBy June 8
First half or full payment optionLast day of February, or April 30 in full
Second halfJune 15
Appeal to County Board of EqualizationBy July 15
Board hearings finishAugust 5
Further appealWithin 30 days of the decision

Real property is revalued in odd-numbered years. Taxes of $25 or less must be paid in full by April 30.

How do you appeal a Delta County valuation?

File with the Assessor between January 1 and June 8 by mail, in person or by phone. The county calls an in-person visit the most effective route and advises appealing early.

  • Gather evidence from the Assessor's sales books and neighborhood sales lists.
  • State why the value is wrong and the value you think is right.
  • Expect the Assessor's response by the last working day of June, and a possible property visit to check size and finish.
  • If you disagree, appeal to the County Board of Equalization by July 15. The Board is made up of the county commissioners, and it must notify you of its decision within five working days.

The county page states that prior tax years cannot be appealed through this process, and that the Assessor cannot consider sales after June 30, 2024. Check the current year's page for updated dates.

Who do you call at Delta County for property tax questions?

The Assessor values property and the Treasurer bills and collects. The Assessor's office is at 375 W. 6th St., Delta, phone 970-874-2120, open 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. weekdays, with shorter hours from May 1 through June 8.

The Treasurer is at 501 Palmer Street, Suite 202, Delta, phone 970-874-2135, open weekdays 8 a.m. to 1 p.m. and 2 p.m. to 5 p.m. Payments can be made in person there or at the County Annex at 196 W. Hotchkiss Avenue in Hotchkiss, by mail to PO Box 580, Grand Junction, or online through GovPros. The mail page says only a USPS postmark counts as proof.

Recording a deed happens at the Clerk and Recorder, 501 Palmer Street, Suite 211, phone 970-874-2150, where the fee is $43 per document.

What happens if Delta County property tax goes unpaid?

Unpaid tax accrues interest at one percent per month, counting part of a month as a full month, under C.R.S. 39-10-104.5. Interest on a missed first half starts March 1, on a missed second half June 16, and on a missed full payment May 1.

Colorado law has a grace window for the first half: if it is paid within 30 days after the treasurer mails the statement, no delinquent interest accrues. Past that, the treasurer can sell the tax lien at the annual sale, and the Delta County pages link rules for that sale. A lien buyer then holds a claim against the house that must be cleared before a clean sale.

A title company asks the Treasurer for a tax certificate before closing, and the county has an online request portal for that. Any unpaid tax comes out of the seller's proceeds at closing.

Can you sell a Delta County house with tax due or a deferral?

Yes. Back taxes, interest and any lien payoff are settled at closing from the sale price, so a seller does not need cash up front.

Anyone using Colorado's property tax deferral program should know a sale triggers repayment. The state treasury says the deferral is recorded as a junior lien, and repayment is due 90 days after a sale or a contract of sale, with interest running from May 1 of the year it was claimed. If an owner dies with no surviving spouse, repayment is due one year after death.

If you are selling a Delta County house that needs work, has a tax lien or came through an estate, we can send a written cash offer for the house as it stands.

More questions about Delta County, CO Property Tax Guide

When is Delta County property tax due?

Taxes can be paid in full by April 30, or in two halves due the last day of February and June 15. Amounts of $25 or less must be paid in full by April 30.

What is the protest deadline for a Delta County property value?

The real property protest deadline is June 8 for the 2026 cycle, by mail, in person or by phone. An appeal to the County Board of Equalization follows by July 15.

What interest does Delta County charge on late property tax?

One percent per month under C.R.S. 39-10-104.5, with part of a month counted as a whole month. It starts March 1 for a late first half, June 16 for a late second half and May 1 for a late full payment.

Where do I pay property tax in Delta County?

Pay at the Treasurer's office at 501 Palmer Street, Suite 202, Delta, at the County Annex in Hotchkiss, by mail to PO Box 580, Grand Junction, or online through GovPros.

Does selling a house in Delta County end the property tax deferral?

A sale or contract of sale makes the state's deferral repayment due within 90 days. The deferral is a recorded junior lien, so it is paid at or soon after closing.

Who records deeds in Delta County?

The Delta County Clerk and Recorder, at 501 Palmer Street, Suite 211, records deeds. The fee listed is $43 per document, plus the state documentary fee when it applies.

Where is Grand County, Colorado, and who lives there?

The county was created on February 2, 1874, carved out of Summit County, and named for Grand Lake and the Grand River, an old name for the upper Colorado River. Its neighbors are Larimer, Gilpin, Boulder, Clear Creek, Summit, Eagle, Jackson and Routt counties.

Census numbers from 2020 show how different the housing picture is from a typical suburb: 16,633 housing units, 7,006 households, and 57.9% of units counted as vacant. Among occupied homes, 69.5% were owner-occupied and 30.5% rented. The median age was 44.0.

What towns and roads make up Grand County?

Grand County has six incorporated towns: Fraser, Granby, Grand Lake, Hot Sulphur Springs, Kremmling and Winter Park. Parshall and Tabernash are census-designated places, and Radium and Troublesome are unincorporated communities.

  • Winter Park, in the southeast, is where the Winter Park Ski Resort is located.

For a seller, the town matters because a property can sit in a town, in an unincorporated area, or next to federal land, and each setting has its own taxing districts. The county Assessor keeps a tax area and tax authority list for sorting this out.

Who handles Grand County property tax?

The Grand County Assessor values every property in the county, and the Grand County Treasurer, who is also the Public Trustee, bills and collects. Both offices are in the same building in Hot Sulphur Springs.

When are Grand County property taxes due, and what are the penalties?

The Treasurer lists the first half due February 28, the full payment due April 30 and the second half due June 15. Interest is charged at 1% per month after each due date, and delinquent notices are mailed July 1.

What does the Grand County Treasurer charge for tax documents?

A Certificate of Taxes Due is $10 in Grand County. This is the paper a title company asks for before a sale closes, so a seller with a cash buyer should expect it to be requested.

Mobile homes are taxed separately from the land unless the title has been purged and the home is permanently set on a foundation. To transfer ownership, all taxes on the mobile home must be paid in full before the Treasurer issues the Certificate of Authenticity, which is then taken with the signed title to the motor vehicle office.

How does the Grand County assessment and appeal process work?

The Assessor's page describes the office as responsible for identifying, classifying and valuing all real and personal property in the county. Colorado revalues property every odd-numbered year, and in the years between, a Notice of Valuation goes out only to owners whose value changed.

The county's published appeal dates need care. The Assessor's page gives June 1 as the real property deadline to appeal to the Assessor and June 30 for personal property, but that page also contains text written for tax year 2014. El Paso County's Assessor, by comparison, lists a May 1 to June 8 appeal period for its own owners. We cannot confirm the current date from the pages we could open, so call the Assessor at 970-725-3060 before relying on either date.

The same page says a change in the residential assessment percentage is not grounds for protest or abatement of taxes. If the Assessor denies a protest or does not answer, the next level is a written appeal to the County Board of Equalization.

What does the Grand County Public Trustee do?

The same office that collects property tax also serves as Public Trustee, so a seller with a mortgage deals with one address in Hot Sulphur Springs. The Treasurer's page says the Public Trustee provides information on the release of deeds of trust and on foreclosures.

When a loan is paid off at closing, the lender requests a release of the deed of trust, and that release clears the lien from the record. The county also posts current Treasurer's deed notices and auction information, and a tax liens page, for anyone who wants to see which parcels have unpaid taxes moving toward sale.

  • Treasurer and Public Trustee phone: 970-725-3061.
  • Tax distribution reports and the mill levy certification (Form DLG 70) are posted on the county site.
  • The Assessor's FAQ section explains how property taxes are determined, what a mill levy is and what an assessment rate is.

What should sellers in Grand County know about vacant and second homes?

Grand County has a high share of vacant units in the Census count, so some owners may receive mail somewhere else. The Treasurer states that taxes are the owner's responsibility whether or not a bill arrives.

  • Keep your address current: the Treasurer's page has a mailing address change form, and the Assessor has a physical address change form.
  • Ask for a Certificate of Taxes Due before listing or accepting an offer.
  • Check whether the home is in a town or an unincorporated area, since the tax area list can differ.
  • If a house has sat with unpaid taxes since the prior year, the Treasurer notes that delinquent taxes may be advertised and sold at the lien sale.

More questions about Grand County, CO Property Tax Guide

When are Grand County property taxes due?

The first half is due February 28, the second half June 15, and a full payment can be made by April 30. Interest is 1% per month after each due date, according to the Treasurer.

What is the appeal deadline in Grand County?

The Assessor's page lists June 1 for real property, but it appears to be older text, and another source gives June 8. Call the Assessor at 970-725-3060 to confirm the current date.

The Treasurer charges $10.00 per certificate.

The office is at 308 Byers Avenue in Hot Sulphur Springs, open Monday to Friday from 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. The phone number is 970-725-3061.

What happens to delinquent Grand County taxes?

Delinquent notices are mailed July 1, payments after September 1 must be cash or cashier's check, and unpaid taxes can be advertised and sold at the annual tax lien sale, usually held in November.

Can I sell a Grand County house with back taxes?

Yes, taxes owed appear on the Certificate of Taxes Due and are normally settled through closing. A buyer paying cash can still close, but the balance and any interest need to be confirmed with the Treasurer.

Jefferson County by the numbers

Which offices handle property tax in Jefferson County, Colorado?

Two county offices split the work. The Assessor sets value and hears appeals, and the Treasurer sends the bills and collects the money. Both are in the Jefferson County Administration and Courts building at 100 Jefferson County Parkway in Golden.

OfficeSuite and phoneRole

The Treasurer's counter is open Monday through Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., and closed on Fridays. The Treasurer cannot raise or lower a bill. The amount comes from three pieces: the Assessor's value and classification, assessment rates set by the state General Assembly, and mill levies set by each taxing entity.

What is Jefferson County like for a homeowner?

Jefferson County runs along the Front Range next to Denver and covers about 774 square miles. Golden is the county seat, Lakewood is the largest city, and the county was reorganized on November 1, 1861 as one of Colorado Territory's original 17.

Cities in the county include Arvada (part), Edgewater, Golden, Lakewood, Littleton (part), Westminster (part), Wheat Ridge, Morrison and Superior (part). Mountain communities such as Conifer and Pine are unincorporated. Your address decides which city, fire district and school district levies show up on the tax notice.

The job base includes the Coors brewery in Golden, the Colorado School of Mines, and the Denver Federal Center in Lakewood, which Wikipedia describes as the largest concentration of federal agencies outside Washington, D.C. Owners near those employers and along the foothills often have very different lots, from small bungalows to acreage in the canyons.

When are Jefferson County property taxes due?

Property tax in Colorado is paid in arrears, so 2025 taxes were payable in 2026. The Treasurer mails notices in late January and the coupons are attached.

2026 payment dateWhat it covers
March 2, 2026First half. February 28 fell on a Saturday, so the county moved the date.
April 30, 2026Full year in one payment
June 15, 2026Second half

U.S. postmarks are accepted for the February, April and June deadlines. When the end of February, April or June lands on a Friday or weekend, the county accepts payment the next business day without delinquent interest. Online payments can take several days to leave your bank account, so do not wait for the last minute.

What happens after a Jefferson County tax bill goes unpaid?

Unpaid real estate taxes are advertised in the fall and then sold as a lien to an investor in November. Delinquent notices are mailed in July, and in August a tax buyer holding an older lien can pay the current year, which adds to that certificate.

  • Early October: the first of three weekly newspaper notices for unpaid real property taxes. The county also says delinquent taxes are advertised for three consecutive weeks beginning in September, and that paying before September 1 avoids the advertising charge.
  • November: the annual tax lien sale, run as an internet sale.
  • Redemption: the owner has three years to redeem the lien by paying the delinquent tax plus accrued interest.
  • After three years: the certificate holder may apply for a public auction of a certificate of option for a treasurer's deed.

Redemption payments must reach the office by 5 p.m. on the last business day of the month, in cash or certified funds. Postmarks do not count, and interest accrues monthly. Call 303-271-8330 for a payoff figure.

How do you appeal a Jefferson County property valuation?

You file with the Assessor between May 1 and June 8, and any mailed appeal must be postmarked by June 8. The county advises filing early because the last days are busy.

  1. Read the Notice of Valuation mailed on May 1 and check value and classification.
  2. Research comparable sales in the Property Records Search, or call 303-271-8666 about inventory for up to three residences.
  3. File the appeal form, mail it, or book an appraiser appointment online.
  4. Expect a Notice of Determination by August 15.
  5. If you still disagree, file with the Board of Equalization by September 15.
  6. The Board must finish hearings by November 1 and notify petitioners within five business days.
  7. A Board decision can be appealed within 30 days.

The dates in steps four through six come from the county's appeal page, which differs from the statewide calendar shown by some other counties, so confirm them with the Assessor if your deadline is close.

How is the current valuation cycle set?

Jefferson County's last reappraisal was 2025, and tax year 2026 is an intervening year. Owners whose value did not change generally did not get a full notice. Postcard notices of value in 2026 went only to owners with changes such as new construction.

The valuation date for this cycle is June 30, 2024, and the Assessor looked only at sales from July 1, 2022 to June 30, 2024. A sale after that date will not show up in the 2025 and 2026 values, so a house that sold higher or lower later is still valued from the earlier data.

What do I need to know about the lien and tax rules when selling?

Because taxes are paid in arrears, a sale that closes in 2026 still leaves a 2026 tax bill that arrives in January 2027. Ask your title or escrow company how that bill will be split, and make sure any past due balance is cleared first.

  • Confirm there is no unpaid balance from earlier years, since a buyer's title search will find a tax lien.
  • Ask the Treasurer about the prepayment cutoff: next year's taxes can be prepaid until noon on the last business day of December.
  • Check whether a Public Trustee release is needed for an old loan.
  • If you are mailing a payment, use certified funds for lien redemption.

How do wildfire rules affect selling a mountain home in Jefferson County?

The Wildfire Resiliency Code, approved March 10, 2026 and effective July 1, 2026, applies to unincorporated properties in the wildland urban interface. It reaches new construction and exterior alterations, including re-roofing and re-siding, and it is not retroactive.

A roof replacement of 25% or more must be a Class A assembly. Defensible space must be inspected by a county approved Wildfire Mitigation Specialist. Re-siding projects that call for Zone 1 standards may use a self-attestation form.

For sellers, that can add cost to a repair list in Conifer, Pine or the foothills. Reading the county's defensible space page before you hire a roofer saves surprises.

Does a cash sale change the tax picture?

A cash sale does not change what is owed to the Treasurer. Any unpaid taxes, a lien or a mortgage balance still has to be settled at or before closing, so an offer from a direct buyer works best when you know your payoff numbers first.

More questions about Jefferson County, CO Property Tax Guide

When is the Jefferson County, CO property tax appeal deadline?

Appeals to the Assessor are due by June 8, with mailed appeals postmarked that day. The window opens May 1 when notices of valuation go out.

When are Jefferson County property taxes due?

For 2025 taxes payable in 2026, the first half was due March 2, the full year April 30 and the second half June 15. Notices mail in late January.

Can I pay my Jefferson County taxes in installments?

Yes. Colorado allows payment in two halves or one full payment, and the county's Important Dates page lists the February, April and June deadlines. The county's tax billing page itself does not describe installments, so confirm with the Treasurer.

How long do I have to redeem a Jefferson County tax lien?

The county says the owner has three years to redeem a tax lien by paying the delinquent taxes and accrued interest. Call 303-271-8330 for the payoff amount.

Who do I call about my Jefferson County property value?

Call the Assessor at 303-271-6511. The Treasurer at 303-271-8330 can explain payments but cannot change a bill.

Adams County by the numbers

Where is Adams County, Colorado, and what does it include?

Adams County sits north and east of Denver, with Brighton as its county seat. According to Wikipedia, the legislature voted to create it in 1901 from part of Arapahoe County, although the article says creation was delayed until November 15, 1902. It was named for Alva Adams, who served as governor from 1887 to 1889.

The county covers 1,184 square miles, nearly all of it land, and the South Platte River runs through it. It borders Weld, Morgan, Washington, Arapahoe, Jefferson and Broomfield, and it touches Denver. It surrounds most of Denver International Airport, which sits inside Denver. About 53 square miles went to Denver in 1989 for the airport's construction.

The 2020 census counted 519,572 residents. Several cities share the county: Arvada, Aurora, Brighton, Commerce City, Federal Heights, Northglenn, Thornton and Westminster, plus the towns of Bennett and Lochbuie. Many of those cities also reach into a neighboring county, so a parcel's address and its county are not always the same thing.

What are the main cities in Adams County and how do they differ?

Thornton is the largest city in the county and the sixth largest in Colorado. It began as a planned community in 1953 and was incorporated on June 12, 1956. It lies in Adams and Weld counties, though every one of its 2020 residents lived on the Adams side.

Commerce City grew from Commerce Town, which voters incorporated in 1952, and it became a city in 1962. Its history is tied to farming, then to a refinery established in 1930 and the Rocky Mountain Arsenal in 1942. Wikipedia describes the Suncor refinery there as the largest in the Rocky Mountain region, and the only entrance to the Rocky Mountain Arsenal National Wildlife Refuge is in the city.

Brighton, the seat, is the center of county government. Aurora is the odd one out: a large share of it lies in Arapahoe County, and a smaller part (47,720 people in 2020) sits in Adams. A seller in Aurora's Adams portion deals with the Adams treasurer, while a neighbor a few blocks away may deal with Arapahoe.

  • Thornton: planned community from the 1950s, with four school districts serving it (Adams 12, Adams 14, Mapleton and Brighton 27J).
  • Commerce City: portions served by Brighton 27J and Adams 14, with Adams City High School as the Adams 14 comprehensive high school.
  • Brighton: county seat since voters chose it in 1904.
  • Federal Heights, Northglenn and Westminster: smaller cities that share the county with Thornton and Brighton.

How do roads and transit shape selling a house in Adams County?

Adams County is crossed by Interstates 25, 70, 76, 225 and 270, several U.S. highways, and the E-470 tollway. Easy access to Denver and the airport is a selling point, but the same highways create noise and traffic that buyers weigh when they tour a house.

Commuter rail also matters in the south and west. The Regional Transportation District's N Line began service on September 21, 2020, with three stations in Thornton: Original Thornton/88th, Thornton Crossroads/104th and Eastlake/124th. A house within a short drive of a station is easier to describe to a buyer than one that needs a long bus connection.

Because the county is large and mixes dense suburbs with the town of Bennett and other rural communities, two sellers in Adams County can have very little in common. A tract house in Thornton, a ranch parcel near Bennett and a bungalow in Commerce City sit under different cities, school districts and tax areas.

When are Adams County property taxes due?

Adams County property tax is due each year on one of two schedules: two halves, or one full payment. The county treasurer lists the first half due February 28, the second half due June 15, and a full payment due April 30. State law (C.R.S. 39-10-104.5) uses the last day of February for the first half, so the date moves in leap years.

The county says only half or full payments are accepted, and partial payments are not. Taxes of $25 or less cannot use the half-payment option and must be paid in one payment by the full-payment date. A payment counts as on time if it carries a U.S. postmark matching the due date.

Colorado collects property tax one year in arrears. The bill you pay in 2027 covers the 2026 tax year. That matters at closing, because the current year's tax is normally prorated between seller and buyer even though no bill has been issued yet.

What does late payment cost in Adams County?

Late payment adds interest of one percent for each month, counted in whole months, and the county publishes a table that shows the running total. For the first half, paying in March adds 1 percent, April 2, May 3, and payment on June 15 or later reaches 4 percent. The second half starts at 1 percent for June 16 to 30 and climbs to 6 percent in November.

State law also lets a treasurer add an administrative charge to small delinquencies. Where delinquent taxes total under $50, a charge of up to $25 can be added, capped so that the total stays at no more than $50. A treasurer may also skip collecting penalty and interest amounts of $50 or less.

How does an Adams County property value appeal work?

You appeal the value of the property, not the tax bill. The Adams County Assessor says appeals cover valuation only, and mill levies vary by tax area. The window runs from May 1 through June 8, and you can file by mail, email, fax or in person.

Only the owner has standing. Anyone else, including an attorney, needs a notarized letter of agency filed with the first appeal. Without it the assessor will not take the appeal, and the owner would have to wait for the next year and file an abatement.

  • Notices of Value are mailed by May 1.
  • The appeal window is May 1 to June 8.
  • Notices of Determination are mailed by August 15.
  • To dispute the determination, mail the completed form to the County Board of Equalization by September 15.
  • Board hearings run September 1 through November 1, and decisions are mailed within five days.
  • After the board rules you have 30 days to go to the Board of Assessment Appeals, district court in Brighton, or binding arbitration.

The county explains that actual value rests on an appraisal as of June 30 of each even-numbered year, using 24 months of sales data. The same page says real property is reappraised every two years and describes that as odd-numbered years, so ask the assessor which cycle applies to your notice.

What happens to unpaid Adams County taxes, and how does it affect a sale?

Unpaid real property tax eventually goes to an online tax lien sale. The treasurer mails delinquent notices in July and lists unpaid real property in a newspaper in September. The county's posted online sale ran from October 7 to November 6, and taxes had to be paid by 5:00 PM on October 31 to avoid the added interest and fees of the sale.

State law requires the treasurer to mail a notice by September 1 to each owner known to owe the previous year's taxes. The notice must give a payment date at least fifteen days out. If you own a house in Adams County and have fallen behind, that letter is the clearest signal that time is short.

Back taxes do not block a sale. They are paid from the proceeds at closing, and the title company can ask the treasurer for a payoff figure. The Adams County Treasurer works from the Adams County Government Center, 4430 South Adams County Parkway in Brighton, and answers at 303-659-2120.

A cash buyer can often close faster than a buyer who needs a lender, which helps when a lien sale date is close. Check the figures with the treasurer first so the payoff is correct.

More questions about Adams County, CO Property Tax Guide

When is the second half of Adams County property tax due?

The second half is due June 15. The first half is due the last day of February, and one full payment is due April 30. A postmark on the due date counts.

Can I pay part of my Adams County tax bill?

No. The county accepts half or full payments only. If your total is $25 or less, you must pay it in a single payment by the full-payment date.

What is the deadline to appeal an Adams County valuation?

The assessor's window runs May 1 through June 8. After a decision, a written appeal to the County Board of Equalization is due by September 15.

Where is the Adams County Treasurer?

The Treasurer's office is at the Adams County Government Center, 4430 South Adams County Parkway, Brighton, CO 80601. The phone number is 303-659-2120.

Which county do I deal with if my Aurora house is on the Adams side?

You deal with Adams County. Aurora lies in Arapahoe, Adams and Douglas counties, and the county where the parcel sits bills the tax. In 2020 about 47,720 Aurora residents lived in Adams County.

What if I owe back taxes and want to sell my Adams County house?

You can still sell. The unpaid tax, interest and fees come out of the sale proceeds at closing, and a payoff figure from the treasurer tells the title company how much that is.

Broomfield County by the numbers

Where is Broomfield County and how big is it?

Broomfield County sits between Denver and Boulder and covers about 33.5 square miles, which makes it the smallest county in Colorado by area. It is also the newest. Wikipedia's Broomfield entry says the county was established on November 15, 2001, as a consolidated city and county, and counts it as Colorado's 64th.

The city itself was incorporated on June 6, 1961, in the southeastern corner of Boulder County. Annexations over the following decades pushed its edges into Adams, Jefferson and Weld counties, and a 1998 state constitutional amendment let the city become its own county after a three year transition. Today the county borders Weld to the northeast, Adams to the southeast, Jefferson to the southwest and Boulder to the northwest.

For a seller, the consolidation matters because one local government plays both roles. The same City and County of Broomfield bills property tax, records deeds and hears valuation protests, so most paperwork on a sale stays inside one building at One DesCombes Drive.

What do the Census Bureau numbers say about Broomfield County homes?

Here are the geography and climate figures we confirmed for Broomfield County.
